cheatsheet.intro: Everything from Lesson 2 on two pages: what each component does, where it runs, the path of one `kubectl apply`, and the commands from the lab.

controlPlane.name: kube-apiserver
controlPlane.role: The front door. Exposes the Kubernetes HTTP API, checks who you are and whether you are allowed, validates what you send and saves it. Scales horizontally: you can run several copies behind a load balancer.
controlPlane.where: Control plane. In kind: static Pod `kube-apiserver-k8s-from-zero-control-plane` in `kube-system`.

controlPlane.name: etcd
controlPlane.role: A consistent, highly available key-value store and the backing store for all cluster data. If etcd is lost without a backup, the cluster forgets everything it was told.
controlPlane.where: Control plane. In kind: static Pod `etcd-k8s-from-zero-control-plane`. Only the API server talks to it.

controlPlane.name: kube-scheduler
controlPlane.role: Watches for Pods that have no node yet and picks one for each, then writes `spec.nodeName`. It only decides; it does not start anything.
controlPlane.where: Control plane. In kind: static Pod `kube-scheduler-k8s-from-zero-control-plane`.

controlPlane.name: kube-controller-manager
controlPlane.role: Runs the built-in controllers (Node, Job, EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount, Deployment, ReplicaSet and more), compiled into one binary and run as one process.
controlPlane.where: Control plane. In kind: static Pod `kube-controller-manager-k8s-from-zero-control-plane`.

controlPlane.name: cloud-controller-manager (optional)
controlPlane.role: Links the cluster to a cloud provider's API, for example to create a cloud load balancer.
controlPlane.where: Control plane, in clouds only. A cluster on your laptop does not have one.

node.name: kubelet
node.role: The node agent. Receives the Pods assigned to its node and makes sure their containers are running and healthy. Does not manage containers that Kubernetes did not create.
node.where: Every node, as a system service. It also runs the static Pod files in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`.

node.name: Container runtime (containerd)
node.role: Actually runs containers. The kubelet talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), a gRPC API, so the runtime is swappable.
node.where: Every node, as a system service. kind nodes use containerd.

node.name: kube-proxy (optional)
node.role: Maintains network rules on the node so that Services work. Some network plugins replace it.
node.where: Usually every node. In kind: a Pod in `kube-system`.

node.name: Add-ons
node.role: Cluster DNS (CoreDNS), the network plugin that gives every Pod an IP (kindnet in kind), and in kind a small storage provisioner.
node.where: Ordinary Pods. In kind, CoreDNS and kindnet are in `kube-system`.

cheatsheet.kindNote: In kind, one node (`k8s-from-zero-control-plane`) is the control plane and also runs your workloads. A kind node is a Docker container, so `docker exec k8s-from-zero-control-plane ...` gets you inside it. kubeadm runs the four control-plane parts as static Pods: Pod files the kubelet reads straight from a folder on the node, without asking the API server.

applySteps.what: Reads `web.yaml`, asks the API server whether Deployment `web` exists (`404 Not Found`), then sends a `POST` (`201 Created`). The API server authenticates you, validates the object and stores it in etcd.
Inside kube-controller-manager. Sees the new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet. Event: `deployment-controller ScalingReplicaSet`.
Sees a ReplicaSet that wants 2 Pods and has 0, so creates two Pod objects: records only, no node, no container. Event: `replicaset-controller SuccessfulCreate`.
Sees Pods with an empty `spec.nodeName`, scores the nodes and binds each Pod by writing a node name into it. Event: `default-scheduler Scheduled`.
Sees Pods assigned to its node and asks containerd to pull the image (or finds it cached), create the container and start it. Events: `kubelet Pulled`, `Created`, `Started`.
Reports the Pod's status, `Running`, back to the API server. `kubectl get pods` now shows it.

cheatsheet.ownership: Each Pod carries an `ownerReference` to its ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet one to its Deployment. That chain is how deleting a Deployment cleans up everything below it.

homework.intro: Use the kind cluster `k8s-from-zero` from the lesson. Names with random suffixes and port numbers will differ on yours. Answers are in the separate answer key.

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: Name the four core control-plane components, and the one optional one.
exercises.a: kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager. The optional one is cloud-controller-manager, which links the cluster to a cloud provider's API.

exercises.q: Which component is the only one that reads and writes etcd? How do the other components learn about changes?
exercises.a: kube-apiserver. The other components never call each other: each talks only to the API server, mostly by watching it for changes and then writing back what it did.

exercises.q: What does every node run? Which node component is optional?
exercises.a: A kubelet and a container runtime (containerd in kind), and usually kube-proxy. kube-proxy is the optional one; some network plugins replace it.

exercises.q: The kubelet talks to the container runtime through an interface. What is it called, what kind of API is it, and why does it matter?
exercises.a: The Container Runtime Interface (CRI), a gRPC API. Because the kubelet only speaks CRI, the runtime is swappable.

exercises.q: What is a static Pod? Which folder holds the static Pod files on a kubeadm node?
exercises.a: A Pod file that the kubelet reads straight from a folder on the node, without asking the API server. The folder is `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`.

exercises.q: Which field does kube-scheduler write into a Pod? Does the scheduler start the container?
exercises.a: `spec.nodeName`. No: the scheduler only decides. The kubelet on that node starts the container.

exercises.q: Name the add-ons in a kind cluster. How do they run?
exercises.a: CoreDNS (cluster DNS), kindnet (the network plugin that gives every Pod an IP) and a small storage provisioner. They run as ordinary Pods.

sections.title: Run this and explain
sections.hint: Run each command on your cluster, then answer.

exercises.q: Run `kubectl get nodes -o wide`. Which column names the container runtime, and what does it say?
exercises.a: `CONTAINER-RUNTIME`. It shows containerd; the lesson's run showed `containerd://2.3.4`. The single node `k8s-from-zero-control-plane` is the control plane and also runs your workloads.

exercises.q: Run `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide`. Which Pod names end in the node name, and why?
exercises.a: `etcd-`, `kube-apiserver-`, `kube-controller-manager-` and `kube-scheduler-k8s-from-zero-control-plane`. They are static Pods, and static Pod names end in the node name. The others (coredns, kindnet, kube-proxy) have random suffixes.

exercises.q: Run `docker exec k8s-from-zero-control-plane ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests` and `docker exec k8s-from-zero-control-plane systemctl is-active kubelet containerd`. What do you see, and what does it tell you about how the node is built?
exercises.a: Four files: `etcd.yaml`, `kube-apiserver.yaml`, `kube-controller-manager.yaml`, `kube-scheduler.yaml`, then `active` twice. The kubelet and containerd are ordinary system services on the node. The four control-plane parts are files in a folder that the kubelet runs as static Pods.

exercises.q: Run `docker exec k8s-from-zero-control-plane crictl ps`. What is `crictl`, and what do the rows show?
exercises.a: A debugging client for any CRI runtime. The rows are the same components (etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, coredns and more), seen from below: containers that containerd runs.

exercises.q: Run `kubectl get leases -n kube-system`. Which two components hold a Lease, and why do they need one?
exercises.a: kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler (you also see an `apiserver-...` lease). In a cluster with several control-plane machines, only one scheduler and one controller manager act at a time; the Lease proves which one is in charge.

exercises.q: Start the event watch in a second terminal, then run `kubectl apply -f web.yaml -v=6 2>&1 | grep 'verb='`. In the kubectl output, why is there a `404 Not Found` before the `201 Created`?
exercises.a: kubectl first asked whether a Deployment called `web` exists. It did not (404), so kubectl sent a `POST` that created it (`201 Created`). Before that, the two `GET .../openapi/v3...` calls fetched the API schema.

exercises.q: From the same run, list the event sources (`FROM` column) in the order they appear, and say what each one did.
exercises.a: `deployment-controller`: ScalingReplicaSet (scaled up a ReplicaSet). `replicaset-controller`: SuccessfulCreate, twice (created two Pods). `default-scheduler`: Scheduled, twice (placed each Pod). `kubelet`: Pulled, Created, Started for each Pod (pulled the image, created and started the container).

exercises.q: Run the two `jsonpath` commands from step 9 of the lesson with one of your Pod names. What three lines come back, and which component wrote the first one?
exercises.a: The node name `k8s-from-zero-control-plane`, then `ReplicaSet/web-<hash>`, then `Deployment/web`. The scheduler wrote `spec.nodeName`. The Pod is owned by the ReplicaSet, which is owned by the Deployment.

exercises.q: Run the `etcdctl ... get /registry/deployments/default/web --keys-only` command from step 10. What comes back, and which component wrote it?
exercises.a: The key `/registry/deployments/default/web`. Your Deployment is a key in etcd, written there by the API server. (For learning only: in real life you never touch etcd by hand.)

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then run it, or check the answer key.

exercises.q: You move `kube-scheduler.yaml` out of `/etc/kubernetes/manifests` and run `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=4`. Predict the `STATUS` of all four `web` Pods, and what `kubectl describe` shows on a new one.
exercises.a: Two old Pods stay `Running`. Two new Pods exist (the controllers still did their part) but stay `Pending`, because nobody gave them a node. `kubectl describe` shows `Node: <none>` and no events at all.

exercises.q: You then move `kube-scheduler.yaml` back into `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`. What happens to the two `Pending` Pods?
exercises.a: The kubelet starts the scheduler again, the scheduler catches up and binds them, and all four Pods become `Running`.

exercises.q: You stop the kubelet with `docker exec k8s-from-zero-control-plane systemctl stop kubelet`. Predict the node's `STATUS` after a short wait, what its conditions say, and whether running containers stop.
exercises.a: The node turns `NotReady` (47 seconds later in the lesson). `kubectl describe node` shows every condition as `Unknown` with `Kubelet stopped posting node status.` Running containers keep running, which is why kubectl still works. `systemctl start kubelet` brings it back to `Ready`.

exercises.q: You run `kubectl delete -f web.yaml`. What happens to the ReplicaSet and the Pods, and what makes that happen?
exercises.a: They are removed too. Each Pod has an `ownerReference` to its ReplicaSet and the ReplicaSet one to its Deployment; that ownership chain is how deleting a Deployment cleans up everything below it.

exercises.q: New Pods stay `Pending` and show no events. Which component do you suspect, and which command checks it?
exercises.a: The scheduler: nothing scheduled the Pods. Check it with `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler`. If it runs, `kubectl describe pod` usually shows a `FailedScheduling` event with the reason.

exercises.q: kubectl prints `The connection to the server ... was refused`. Give the two likely causes from the lesson.
exercises.a: kubectl cannot reach the API server: the cluster is stopped, or kubectl points at the wrong cluster.
